title: Enough for Christians; moderation in the schools
source_text: LXXXIII. Ista quae nullus in dubium vocat, Christianis omnibus meo judicio sufficere deberent, absque ulteriori & curiosiori investigatione, tum intimae naturae libertatis humanae, tum modi quo gratia in nobis operatur, & quo etiam ejus efficacia cum arbitrii nostri libertate concilianda est; de quibus nulla diserta, clara, & expressa extant Scripturae oracula. Si quis tamen pertendat licere de his rebus ulterius & accuratius in Scholis Philosophari, optandum saltem esset id fieri summa cum animi moderatione, & agnitione syncera propriae nostrae caliginis atque ignorantiae in rebus tam arduis quae omnem ex disputationibus, circa materiam per se tam gravem atque difficilem, acerbitatem tolleret, & animos ad mutuam Christianam & fraternam tolerantiam formaret. Quod Deus per eandem illam suam gratiam in iis qui Scholis Christianis praesunt, praestare velit.
pass_a_gloss: LXXXIII. Those things which no one calls in doubt, ought in my judgment to suffice all Christians, without further & more curious investigation, both of the inmost nature of human freedom, and of the manner in which grace works in us, & in which also its efficacy is to be reconciled with the freedom of our choice; about which there exist no distinct, clear, & express oracles of Scripture. Yet if anyone maintains that it is lawful to philosophize about these things further & more exactly in the Schools, it would at least be desirable that it be done with the greatest moderation of mind, & sincere acknowledgment of our own darkness and ignorance in things so arduous which would take away all bitterness from disputes, on a matter in itself so weighty and difficult, & would form minds to mutual Christian & brotherly toleration. Which may God be pleased to bring about through that same grace of his in those who preside over the Christian Schools.
pass_b_english: Thesis LXXXIII. In my judgment these points, which no one questions, ought to be enough for all Christians, without further and more curious inquiry into the inmost nature of human freedom, into how grace works in us, or into how its efficacy is to be reconciled with the freedom of our choice; on these Scripture gives no distinct, clear and express pronouncements.

If anyone insists that it is permissible to philosophize about these matters further and more precisely in the schools, it would at least be desirable to do so with the greatest restraint, and with a sincere admission of our own darkness and ignorance in such hard matters. That would take all bitterness out of the debates on a subject so weighty and difficult in itself, and would train minds to mutual Christian and brotherly tolerance. May God, by that same grace of his, be pleased to bring this about in those who preside over the Christian schools.
